kits.familyName: Using time well after finishing early
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You finished your assigned tasks an hour early, and {lead|the} is in a long meeting.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have finished everything on your list early. {Lead|the} is in a meeting for the next hour.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody will notice if you just take it easy.
{coworker3} jokes that finishing early means you earned a long break.
detail: The {area} is quieter than usual today.
It is the middle of the shift.

tiers.1: A hazard someone could walk into comes before any other task.
tiers.2: Your own error should be fixed before it causes problems for others.
tiers.3: Stay within what you are allowed to do, even when trying to help.
tiers.4: Helping a teammate who is behind comes before improvements.
tiers.5: Ideas for improvement can be raised once the urgent needs are met.

fact: On your way back from the break room, you notice {hazard}.
issues.action: Mark off the hazard so nobody walks into it, and report it right away.
issues.brief: mark off the hazard and report it
issues.reason: Taking initiative includes acting on hazards you notice. Marking it off protects people until it is fixed.
issues.lesson: When you spot a hazard, protect people from it and report it; do not assume someone else will.

shortcut.text: Mention the hazard to {lead|the} after the meeting ends.
shortcut.brief: mention the hazard after the meeting
shortcut.why: Someone could be hurt in the next hour. A hazard needs action now, not later.
shortcut.mis: Problems can wait until the supervisor is free.

fact: You realize an entry you made in {record|the} this morning has the wrong date.
issues.short: the wrong date in your entry
issues.action: Correct your entry in {record|the} the usual way and note that you changed it.
issues.brief: correct your entry and note the change
issues.reason: Fixing your own mistake without being asked keeps the record reliable and shows self-direction.
issues.lesson: Correct your own mistakes as soon as you find them, without waiting to be told.

shortcut.text: Leave the wrong date, since nobody has noticed it.
shortcut.why: Others rely on the record. An error left in place can cause confusion later.
shortcut.mis: A mistake nobody noticed does not need fixing.

fact: The obvious next task needs a certification you do not have.
issues.action: Leave the certified task for qualified staff and pick another useful task.
issues.brief: leave the certified task and pick another
issues.reason: Initiative means finding useful work within what you are allowed to do. Certified tasks are restricted for good reasons.
issues.lesson: Take initiative within the limits of your role and training.

shortcut.text: Do the certified task anyway, since you have watched it done many times.
shortcut.why: Watching is not certification. Doing restricted work can cause harm and break workplace rules.
shortcut.mis: Having seen a task done is enough to do it.

fact: Nobody has told you what to do next.
clear: {Lead|the} left a list of extra tasks for anyone who finishes early.
issues.done: a task list was already left for you
issues.short: not knowing what to do next
issues.action: Check the task board or ask {coworker} what needs doing.
issues.brief: check the task board or ask {coworker}
issues.reason: Finding out what needs doing, instead of waiting to be told, is the core of self-direction.
issues.lesson: When your work is done, look for what needs doing instead of waiting to be told.

shortcut.text: Wait at your station until {lead|the} comes out of the meeting.
shortcut.why: An hour of waiting wastes time that could help the team. You can find work without your supervisor.
shortcut.mis: You should only work on what you are told to do.

fact: {coworker2} is falling behind on a rush order that you know how to help with.
issues.action: Offer to help {coworker2} with the rush order.
issues.reason: Seeing where help is needed and offering it moves the team's work forward.
issues.lesson: Notice where your help is needed and offer it.

shortcut.text: Leave {coworker2} to it, since your own work is finished.
shortcut.why: The team's work is not finished. Helping a teammate who is behind is a good use of spare time.
shortcut.mis: Once your own work is done, the rest is not your concern.

fact: You notice that {equipment|the} jams at about the same time every afternoon.
issues.action: Write down when the jams happen and share the pattern with {lead|the} later.
issues.brief: write down when it jams and share the pattern
issues.reason: Noticing a pattern and recording it gives the right people what they need to fix the cause.
issues.lesson: Record patterns you notice so the right person can act on them.

shortcut.text: Take {equipment|the} apart yourself to find out what is wrong.
shortcut.why: Repairs may need training or permission. Recording and reporting the pattern is the useful step.

proceed.text: Start another useful task and tell {lead|the} what you picked up.
proceed.why: Nothing more urgent needs attention, so starting useful work and keeping the lead informed is the best use of the time.
proceed.lesson: Use spare time on useful work and keep your supervisor informed.

generic.text: Spend the hour on your phone, since your assigned work is done.
generic.why: The workday is not over. Using spare time well is part of being dependable and self-directed.
generic.mis: Finishing your list early means the rest of the time is yours.

generic.text: Interrupt {lead|the}'s meeting to ask what to do next.
generic.why: Interrupting a meeting for something you can figure out yourself is not necessary.
generic.mis: Only a supervisor can say what needs doing.

overcaution.text: Wait until {lead|the} confirms the list is still current before starting.
overcaution.why: The list was left for exactly this situation. Waiting wastes the time it was meant to fill.
overcaution.mis: Instructions always need to be reconfirmed.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You finished your work early, and {lead|the} is unavailable.

unclear: You are not sure what is most needed right now.
ownerror: You spot a mistake in something you filled out this morning.
teammate: {coworker2} is struggling with a rush order.

steps.text: Fix the mistake you made earlier
Check the task board for what is needed
Tell {lead|the} what you did with the time

rel: Your own mistake should be fixed before you move on.
You need to know which task is needed before starting it.
A teammate's rush order comes before optional extra tasks.
You report what you did after doing it.
Your report should include the correction.
process.lesson: Fix your own errors, find what is needed, help where it counts, then report.

title: Your note to {lead|the}
intro: You are leaving {lead|the} a note about what you did after finishing early. Check it first.
doc.lesson: A self-directed worker reports what they did, stays within their role and flags what needs attention.

lines.text: I finished my assigned list about an hour early.
I helped {coworker2} finish the rush order.
lines.fine: Reports help given where it was needed.

lines.text: Then I restocked the {area} from the extra-tasks list.
lines.fine: Chose a useful task from the list.

bad.text: Then I did the certified equipment check, since I have watched it many times.
bad.why: Certified tasks are restricted to qualified staff. Watching does not qualify you.

lines.text: I marked off {hazard} and reported it to {coworker3}, who was in charge while you were out.
lines.fine: Acted on a hazard and reported it to the person covering.

bad.text: I noticed {hazard}, but I left it for you to deal with later.
bad.why: A hazard can hurt someone before the supervisor returns. It needed to be marked off and reported right away.

lines.text: {Equipment|the} jammed three afternoons this week around 2 p.m.; I wrote down the times.
lines.fine: Records a pattern for the right person to act on.

bad.text: {Equipment|the} kept jamming, so I took it apart to look; it is in pieces on the bench.
bad.why: Taking equipment apart without permission or training can damage it and leave it out of service. Recording the pattern is the right step.

lines.text: I corrected the wrong date I had entered in {record|the} and initialed the change.
lines.fine: Fixed own mistake and marked the change.

bad.text: I noticed a wrong date I had entered, but left it, since nobody had spotted it.
bad.why: Leaving a known error in a record is not acceptable; it should be corrected.

review.notes: Uses the bundle hazard slot (recognizable hazards). 'outside' and 'unclear' share tier 3 and never co-occur.

kits.familyName: Working through a new task with little supervision
setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} gave you written instructions for a task you have never done and will be out until the end of the day.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are doing a new task alone from written instructions while {lead|the} is out.
pressure: {coworker3} tells you to just do your best and not bother anyone.
{coworker3} says asking questions makes new people look weak.
detail: The instructions are two pages long.
You have the work area to yourself today.

tiers.1: A step that could damage equipment comes before everything else.
tiers.2: A schedule problem should be raised as early as possible.
tiers.3: Fill gaps in the instructions before they cause rework.
tiers.4: After real effort, asking for help beats staying stuck.
tiers.5: Routine updates come after urgent questions.

fact: One step could damage {equipment|the} if done wrong, and you do not understand how to do it.
issues.short: the risky step you do not understand
issues.action: Pause at that step and call or message {lead|the} for guidance before doing it.
issues.brief: pause and contact {lead|the} about that step
issues.reason: Working independently does not mean guessing on a step that could cause damage. A quick question prevents an expensive mistake.
issues.lesson: Work independently, but ask before a step where a mistake could cause damage.

shortcut.text: Try the step carefully and see what happens.
shortcut.brief: try the step and see what happens
shortcut.why: Experimenting on a step that could damage equipment risks a costly mistake. A quick question is cheaper.
shortcut.mis: Figuring it out alone is always the self-directed choice.

fact: At your current pace, the task will not be done by the end of the day as {lead|the} expects.
clear: {Lead|the} already moved the due time to tomorrow morning.
issues.done: the due time was already moved to tomorrow
issues.action: Message {lead|the} now that the task is running behind and why.
issues.brief: tell {lead|the} the task is running behind
issues.reason: Early warning lets the lead plan around the delay or send help. Waiting until the end of the day removes those options.
issues.lesson: Tell your supervisor about delays as soon as you see them coming.

shortcut.text: Say nothing and hope you can speed up later.
shortcut.brief: say nothing and try to speed up
shortcut.why: If you cannot catch up, the lead learns about the delay too late to adjust.
shortcut.mis: Raising a delay makes you look bad, so it is better to hide it.

fact: The written instructions do not say how the finished work should be labeled.
clear: {coworker} showed you how past finished work was labeled.
issues.done: you already found out how past work was labeled
issues.action: Look at how similar past work was labeled and follow that example.
issues.brief: follow how past work was labeled
issues.reason: Using an existing example is a sensible, independent way to fill a gap in the instructions.
issues.lesson: Fill gaps in instructions by applying solutions that already exist.

shortcut.text: Leave the work unlabeled until {lead|the} returns tomorrow.
shortcut.why: Unlabeled work can get lost or mixed up. A past example gives you a reasonable answer now.
shortcut.mis: If the instructions do not say, the step can be skipped.

fact: You have tried two ways to fix a formatting problem, and neither worked.
issues.short: the formatting problem you are stuck on
issues.action: Ask {coworker} for help, explaining what you have already tried.
issues.brief: ask {coworker} for help with what you tried
issues.reason: You have made a real effort. Asking for help now, with what you tried, saves time and respects the helper's time.
issues.lesson: Try on your own first, then ask for help and explain what you tried.

shortcut.text: Keep trying new things on your own for the rest of the day.
shortcut.why: Spending the day stuck wastes time. Self-direction includes knowing when to ask.
shortcut.mis: Asking for help means you are not self-directed.

fact: {Lead|the} asked for a short update when you reached the halfway point, and you just did.
clear: You already sent {lead|the} the halfway update.
issues.done: the halfway update was already sent
issues.action: Send {lead|the} a short message saying you have reached the halfway point.
issues.reason: The lead asked for this update. Sending it keeps them informed without needing to check on you.
issues.lesson: Keep your supervisor informed the way they asked, especially when working alone.

shortcut.text: Skip the update, since things are going fine.
shortcut.why: The lead asked for it. Skipping it leaves them wondering how the task is going.
shortcut.mis: Updates only matter when something is wrong.

proceed.text: Continue through the instructions on your own, step by step.
proceed.why: Nothing in the situation needs a question or a warning, so steady independent work is exactly what the lead expects.
proceed.lesson: When the path is clear, keep working independently and steadily.

generic.text: Stop and wait for {lead|the} to return before doing anything else.
generic.why: Stopping all work for a whole day wastes time when much of the task can go ahead.
generic.mis: Without a supervisor present, it is safer to do nothing.

generic.text: Ask {coworker3} to finish the task for you.
generic.why: The task was given to you. Handing it off without a reason skips the chance to learn and may overload a coworker.
generic.mis: Handing off unfamiliar work is a good way to avoid mistakes.

overcaution.text: Message {lead|the} for approval before each step.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation needs a question. Asking at every step defeats the purpose of working independently.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, doing an unfamiliar task from written instructions while {lead|the} is out.

gap: The instructions leave out how to label the finished work.
update: {Lead|the} wants a message once you are halfway done.

steps.text: Read all of the instructions first
Find an example of past labeling
Complete the first half of the task

rel: Reading the whole set first helps you spot problems early.
Reading the instructions is how you notice what they leave out.
You need the labeling example before you label.
The halfway message comes once you are halfway done.
The update is meant to arrive before the task is complete.
The second half follows the first.
process.lesson: Read everything first, fill gaps with existing examples, and keep your supervisor updated along the way.

title: Your message to {lead|the}
intro: You are about to message {lead|the} about the new task. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Good independent work includes clear, timely, honest messages about progress and problems.

lines.text: Halfway update: the first half is finished.
I labeled the finished pieces the same way as last month's work.
lines.fine: Filled a gap by following an existing example.

bad.text: The instructions did not say how to label things, so I skipped labeling.
bad.why: Skipping a needed step because instructions are unclear can cause lost or mixed-up work. An existing example would have filled the gap.

lines.text: At this pace I will need about an hour tomorrow morning to finish.
lines.fine: Warns about a delay early and specifically.

lines.text: Before step 6, could you tell me how to set the guide? I do not want to damage it.
lines.fine: Asks before a step that could cause damage.

bad.text: I was not sure how to do step 6, so I tried a few settings until one seemed to work.
bad.why: Guessing on a step that could damage equipment risks costly harm. That step called for a question first.

lines.text: {coworker} helped with the formatting after I had tried two fixes.
lines.fine: Asked for help after real effort and says so.

bad.text: I spent three hours alone on the formatting so I would not bother anyone.
bad.why: The task is already running behind. Hours stuck without asking made the delay worse; asking earlier was the better choice.

lines.text: I will keep going with the second half now.

review.notes: Self-direction with appropriate help-seeking; tiers favour preventing damage and early communication.
